cells.tense: You are gathering the loose threads right now, and you can feel them coming together.
cells.ask: Name the two lines in front of you, on paper, and the order between them, then stop before you add a third.
cells.core:
You can gather what is scattered. Not by forcing it — you have the pattern in your hands and the pieces fall in behind it. You see how the parts connect before anyone has said how, and then the saying is just cleanup.

That is why what you collect holds. There is a fairness running under it: you pick up a thread because it matters, and you put it where it belongs rather than where it serves you. Nothing is being arranged to impress anyone. The order you make is the order that is there, and people can feel it when they stand on it.
cells.sheetLine: You can feel the shape of it, and you can say it plain.

cells.tense: You will have it all aligned, and you are already bracing for the version where you don't.
cells.ask: Write the one line you are most sure of, put it down after ten minutes, and leave the rest unarranged until tomorrow.
cells.core:
There is a full picture ahead of you — every loose end settled, every piece in its place — and you are trying to pull the present into that picture before it is ready. So the gathering turns into forcing. New information arrives and you test it against the shape you have already committed to, not the one forming under your hands.

The trouble is that a pattern you insist on stops being one. What you are building needs a little slack to arrive, and tightening it early costs you the very alignment you are after. The grip is doing the opposite of what the grip is for.
cells.sheetLine: You are braced for a full picture that has not arrived yet.

cells.tense: You stopped gathering the threads, and you are still standing where you left them.
cells.ask: Tell one person one small thing you have sorted out, and let how they take it stand as enough.
cells.core:
In its own shape this is a live thing handed back and forth — you see how the pieces fit and you say the shape out loud, and someone else picks it up and stands on it. The pattern holds because it is shared, and the sharing is what keeps it from drifting.

That is not the way it is sitting. You can see how the pieces fit, but the collecting has gone quiet, and so has the saying. The pattern is intact and it stays on the table, unspoken, while the strands sit where they landed. What you have is real and it has not gone anywhere. Seeing the shape is not the same as holding it; holding takes another person. That is the missing half.
cells.sheetLine: What you know is intact. The saying of it stopped.

cells.tense: You are already arranging what people call their own story, and you have not said it is you.
cells.ask: Tell one memory or one story you carry to someone new, and say plainly that it came through you.
cells.core:
Done well, this is a live thread — you hold a story because it means something, and you pass it on in a way that fits whoever is in front of you. It stays yours and it stays theirs, and it lands because it is the real thing.

What has not followed is the claim. You are shaping what those around you take as the truth of a situation — how it is told, which parts matter, what gets left out. That work is happening now, quietly, and it holds people together. But you speak of it as how things are, or as what someone else figured out, or as just the way it gets said. Which pieces stay and which ones go is the thing that makes the story land at all. Somebody is doing that. It is you.
cells.sheetLine: You are already shaping the story. You have not claimed it.
